## Decision: The proposed design is **not sufficient** as stated

**Premise correction.** "Stable snapshot + no phantoms" is true under Repeatable Read (it prohibits all standard phenomena except serialization anomaly, going beyond the SQL standard's minimum — Table 13.1), but a stable snapshot does **not** make concurrent decisions equivalent to serial execution. The docs warn directly: "the view will not necessarily always be consistent with some serial execution" and attempts to enforce business rules at this level "are not likely to work correctly without careful use of explicit locks." Read/write-dependency cycles (write skew) defeat exactly the "read invariant, then update different rows" pattern described (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html#XACT-REPEATABLE-READ; https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/applevel-consistency.html).

**Standard vs. implementation.** The SQL standard defines each level's phenomena as *minimum* protections; PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read (Snapshot Isolation) exceeds that minimum by preventing phantom reads, yet still permits serialization anomalies. Only Serializable (implemented via Serializable Snapshot Isolation with nonblocking predicate locks) ensures committed transactions' effects equal some serial order (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE).

**Isolation choice.** For a cross-row invariant read-then-write, use Serializable, *or* Repeatable Read plus explicit blocking — `SELECT FOR UPDATE/SHARE`/`LOCK TABLE` (with locks taken *before* queries, since the RR snapshot freezes at the first query) — ideally reduced to what integrity requires (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/applevel-consistency.html#SERIALIZABLE-CONSISTENCY, #NON-SERIALIZABLE-CONSISTENCY). A single write-only transaction that never re-evaluates multi-row invariants can stay at Repeatable Read.

**Recovery and retry ownership.** PostgreSQL offers **no automatic retry facility**: "It is important to retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue… PostgreSQL does not offer an automatic retry facility, since it cannot do so with any guarantee of correctness" (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/mvcc-serialization-failure-handling.html#MVCC-SERIALIZATION-Failure-HANDLING). Statement-level replay is therefore incorrect.

**Retry unit and codes.**
- Retry the **whole transaction** (all reads + decisions + writes), owned by the **application** (or its framework-wrapper at transaction boundaries).
- Retry `40001` (serialization_failure) unconditionally; `40P01` (deadlock) is advisable.
- Unique-key `23505`/exclusion `23P01`: **not** an unconditional bucket. Though sometimes an undetected serialization failure ("the server will not 'see' the connection between the inserted value and the previous reads"), they "might represent persistent error conditions," so retry only after cause inspection (same page). Serializable can even raise unique violations despite prior existence checks when not all inserters follow the check-first protocol (transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE).

**Three-attempt commit promise.** Cannot be honestly made. The docs state "multiple retries may be needed" under high contention, possibly "many attempts," and pinned prepared transactions can block progress indefinitely (failure-handling page). A bounded-attempts SLA is a product policy choice, not a PostgreSQL guarantee — document it as best-effort with fallback behavior (UNVERIFIED as a universal guarantee; a load/contention benchmark of these workers would only bound observed, not guaranteed, attempt counts).

**Narrow changes that matter:** switch the invariant pattern to Serializable (or RR + pre-snapshot explicit locks); move retry to transaction scope, driven by SQLSTATE code; make unique-violation retries conditional on cause.
